title: Stability & Skipping
scopeHtml: Stable/unstable/immutable, @Stable/@Immutable contracts, strong skipping, lambda memoization, compiler reports, stability config, immutable collections, and the production traps around them. Version facts follow developer.android.com (strong skipping default from Kotlin 2.0.20; stability config file from Compose Compiler 1.5.5).

questions.promptHtml: What does "stable" mean in Compose, and why does the compiler care about it?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Stability is the vocabulary behind every recomposition-performance discussion. They want to see whether you know it is a skipping decision input, not a correctness property.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Stability is the compiler's promise about a type: if two instances are equals(), they are interchangeable, and if a public property ever changes, Compose gets notified. The compiler uses it to decide whether a composable can be skipped when its parameters look unchanged. Stable params are compared with equals(). Unstable ones, in the old model, meant the function always re-ran. Since strong skipping, they are compared by reference instead.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
When a parent recomposes, it re-invokes the child with parameters. For each child the compiler-generated code asks: did any parameter change since last time? To answer safely it needs a rule for "changed".

  • Stable type: equals() is trustworthy and mutation is observable (via snapshot state). So "equal now" means "renders the same" and skipping is safe.
  • Unstable type: the compiler cannot prove that. A var field mutated silently would not trigger recomposition, and equals() might say "equal" while content differs.

The compiler infers this per class and writes $stable info plus $changed bit-masks into every composable signature. Primitives, String, function types and enums are stable; Modifier is stable; State<T> is stable.

parent recomposes
   -> call child(p1, p2)
        stable param   : p1 == old p1 (equals)
        unstable param : legacy: "assume changed"  | strong skipping: p2 === old p2
   -> all same? skip child body : run body

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Inferred stable: all vals of stable types, in a module compiled with the Compose compiler
data class Price(val amount: Long, val currency: String)

// Inferred unstable: var of non-state type
data class Cart(var items: Int)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Thinking unstable means "buggy" or "slow". It only changes how the skip comparison works.
  • Thinking @Stable makes a class stable. It is an unchecked promise.
  • Conflating stability with data class.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Is String stable? → Yes, immutable primitives-like types are stable.
  2. Is a lambda stable? → Yes, the compiler always treats function types as stable; the issue was allocation, not stability (see strong skipping questions).
  3. Who consumes stability info at runtime? → The generated $changed mask and Composer.changed() calls inside the composable.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "Stable means it does not change, so Compose can skip." Senior: states the contract (equals reliability plus change notification), links it to the $changed comparison, and notes strong skipping changed what unstable costs.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Teams chase "unstable" lines in reports without checking whether the composable even recomposes often. Knowing it is a skip input prevents that wasted work.

questions.promptHtml: What is the difference between @Stable and @Immutable, and what happens if you annotate wrongly?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests whether you treat annotations as contracts and know their failure mode.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: @Immutable promises that all public properties never change after construction. @Stable is weaker: properties may change, but every change is observable by Compose (usually via mutableStateOf), equals() is consistent, and results of same inputs are the same. Both make the compiler treat the class as stable. They do not enforce anything. If I lie, the UI shows stale data because Compose skips a composable whose parameter silently mutated.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Compiler behavior is identical for both today: type becomes stable and is compared with equals(). The difference is documentation of intent for humans and future optimizations. The contract for @Stable:

  1. equals(a, b) always returns the same result for the same two instances.
  2. If a public property changes, composition is notified.
  3. All public property types are stable.

A class that holds var count by mutableStateOf(0) fits @Stable: change is observable, readers invalidate themselves. A plain var does not.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@Immutable
data class Banner(val title: String, val url: String)

@Stable
class CounterState {
    var count by mutableIntStateOf(0)   // observable mutation
        private set
    fun inc() { count++ }
}

@Stable
class Broken { var count = 0 }          // contract violation: silent mutation

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Annotating a class holding MutableList as @Immutable.
  • Believing the annotation gets checked. It does not.
  • Annotating classes that are already inferred stable (noise).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Which is safer for a mutable holder? → @Stable with state-backed properties.
  2. Do the annotations affect equals()? → No; they change which comparison Compose chooses.
  3. Is @Stable on an interface meaningful? → Yes, it declares that all implementors must honor the contract; useful where inference is impossible.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "Immutable never changes, stable may change." Senior: the three-part contract, the "unchecked like !!" framing, and the rule of annotating only when inference fails AND instances are re-created with equal values.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A @Stable model with a plain var field caused a screen that never updated after a background refresh; the fix was moving the field into mutableStateOf.

questions.promptHtml: Why does the Compose compiler treat List<T> as unstable, and is that still a problem today?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: The single most common stability question. Separates people who memorized "use ImmutableList" from those who know the current guidance.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: List, Set and Map are interfaces. A List<String> may actually be an ArrayList mutated elsewhere, and the compiler only sees the declared type, so it marks it unstable. Before strong skipping that made any composable with a List param non-skippable. With strong skipping on (default from Kotlin 2.0.20) it is skippable and compared by reference, so it is only a problem if you create a new list instance on every emission.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
The compiler cannot prove immutability from a read-only interface (val s: Set<String> = mutableSetOf("a") is legal). So List<Snack> is unstable even if Snack is stable, and so is any class containing a List.

Cases:

Mode List param, same instance List param, new equal instance
Legacy (no strong skipping) recomposes (not skippable) recomposes
Strong skipping skips (===) recomposes
ImmutableList / config-stable skips (equals) skips if elements equal, but O(n) compare each pass

Official guidance now prefers preserving the instance (cache in ViewModel or remember) over wrapping.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Allocates a new list each recomposition of the caller -> defeats === under strong skipping
@Composable fun Screen(items: List<Item>) {
    ItemList(items.filter { it.visible })
}

// Fix: keep the instance stable
@Composable fun ScreenFixed(items: List<Item>) {
    val visible = remember(items) { items.filter { it.visible } }
    ItemList(visible)
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Wrapping every list in ImmutableList without measuring.
  • Building the list in the composable body.
  • Thinking listOf() makes the type stable.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What does ImmutableList change? → Marks the param stable so equals() is used; cost O(n) per compare.
  2. Does data class with a List field stay unstable? → Yes.
  3. How do you keep the same list instance across emissions? → Cache transformations in ViewModel/remember, use distinctUntilChanged, avoid re-mapping unchanged data.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "Use ImmutableList." Senior: explains why, states that under strong skipping the real bug is instance churn, and quantifies the O(n) equals trade-off.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A feed rebuilt its List<UiModel> with map {} in a combine on every tick; fixing upstream allocation removed recomposition without any annotations.

questions.promptHtml: How do you generate and read the Compose compiler reports to find stability problems?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Practical tooling knowledge; shows you diagnose instead of guess.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: I enable reportsDestination and metricsDestination in the composeCompiler Gradle block, build a release variant, and read <module>-composables.txt and -classes.txt. In composables I look for restartable skippable and for params marked unstable. In classes I see which field made a class unstable. I only act on composables that actually recompose hot, confirmed in Layout Inspector or a benchmark.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Setup (Compose Compiler Gradle plugin):

// module build.gradle.kts
composeCompiler {
    reportsDestination = layout.buildDirectory.dir("compose_compiler")
    metricsDestination = layout.buildDirectory.dir("compose_compiler")
}

Run on a release build (docs say so for accurate results; debug can differ). Outputs: *-classes.txt, *-composables.txt, *-composables.csv, plus a metrics JSON with counts.

Reading a composable entry:

restartable skippable fun HighlightedSnacks(
  stable index: Int
  unstable snacks: List<Snack>
  stable onSnackClick: Function1<Long, Unit>
)
  • restartable: has its own recompose scope.
  • skippable: can be skipped if params compare equal. Without strong skipping, the unstable param would drop this tag.
  • unstable snacks: compared by === under strong skipping. Classes report shows the cause: unstable val tags: Set<String> and <runtime stability> = Unstable.

sections.label: Code
sections.html: (build config above)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Reading reports from a debug build.
  • Treating every unstable as a bug under strong skipping.
  • Forgetting reports are per module; the data module needs its own run.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What does runtime stability mean? → Stability decided at runtime (e.g., type parameters), as opposed to compile-time known.
  2. What is non-restartable? → No scope; cannot be recomposed independently (inline/@NonRestartableComposable).
  3. How do you automate this in CI? → Parse the CSV, diff skippable counts between builds, alert on regressions in chosen hot modules.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "Turn on reports and look for unstable." Senior: reads in conjunction with Layout Inspector counts, knows strong skipping changes the meaning of the output, and ties fixes to benchmarks.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A report diff after a dependency bump showed 40 composables flipped from skippable to not, revealing a model module that lost its Compose plugin.

questions.promptHtml: Walk me through how the compiler infers whether a class is stable.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests mechanism knowledge beyond "data classes are stable".

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A class is inferred stable when it is final-ish in shape: all public properties are val (or var backed by Compose state), and every property type is itself stable. Anything with a mutable var, a collection interface, an interface type, or a type from a module not compiled with the Compose compiler makes it unstable. Annotations and config file entries override inference. Generics are decided by type arguments.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Rules in rough order:

  1. @Stable/@Immutable annotation, or listed in the stability config: stable (override).
  2. Primitives, String, function types, Unit, enums: stable.
  3. Class with any non-private mutable var (not State): unstable.
  4. All fields stable: stable. One unstable field poisons the class.
  5. Interface / abstract / unknown-implementation types: unstable unless annotated (the compiler cannot see the implementation).
  6. Classes from another module: only stable if that module was compiled with the Compose compiler (so stability metadata exists) or annotated/configured.
  7. Generic Box<T>: stable depending on T (shown as runtime stability in reports). Also in Kotlin 2.0, stability metadata is generated for classes when compiled with the plugin; an uncompiled module gives no such metadata.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
data class A(val id: Long, val name: String)      // stable
data class B(val id: Long, val tags: List<String>) // unstable (List)
data class C(val a: A, var n: Int)                 // unstable (var)
data class D(val a: A, val n: State<Int>)          // stable

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Assuming a private var always matters (private mutable state is not part of the public contract; verify with the reports for your compiler version).
  • Assuming Kotlin data class or Serializable implies anything.
  • Forgetting an Instant/LocalDate from java.time is unstable (not annotated).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why is java.time.LocalDateTime unstable? → Not compiled with Compose compiler and unknown immutability; add to the config file.
  2. Are type params stable? → Depends on the argument; marked runtime.
  3. Does object / companion count? → Treated by its fields; stateless ones are stable.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "val and primitives are stable." Senior: lists rule precedence, cross-module metadata, and verifies in classes.txt.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Domain Instant fields in a UI model quietly made a whole list item type unstable until added to the stability config.

questions.promptHtml: What does strong skipping mode change, and when is it on by default?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Direct test of whether you are current. Many answers still describe pre-2024 behavior.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Strong skipping does two things: every restartable composable becomes skippable even with unstable params, and every lambda inside a composable is auto-wrapped in remember keyed by its captures. Unstable params are compared by ===, stable ones by equals(). It is default-on from Kotlin 2.0.20 with the Compose compiler Gradle plugin; before that it was opt-in via enableStrongSkippingMode = true.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Before: skippability needed all params stable, so one List param meant the function always ran when the parent recomposed. After: skip decision is per param by type.

              stable param        unstable param
legacy        equals()            not skippable
strong skip   equals()            ===

Non-restartable composables stay non-skippable. Opt out per function with @NonSkippableComposable. APK impact is small (docs: about 4 kB in Now in Android). Version nuance: sources disagree on exact introduction (flag appeared experimentally around compiler 1.5.4; Kotlin 2.0.0 had it off; default on in 2.0.20). I cite the official docs: 2.0.20. Verify against your project's actual Kotlin version.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
composeCompiler {
    // Kotlin < 2.0.20 only; default on from 2.0.20
    enableStrongSkippingMode = true
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Believing it makes everything stable. It changes comparison, not stability.
  • Believing it fixes new-instance-per-emission patterns.
  • Assuming the flag name is unchanged forever (newer plugin versions use feature flags; verify).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does it change @Stable semantics? → No, annotated classes still use equals().
  2. What opts out? → @NonSkippableComposable; @DontMemoize for lambdas.
  3. What are the risks of enabling it on an old codebase? → Skipping that was previously impossible now happens; code that relied on accidental recomposition (reads of non-state mutable data) can show stale UI.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "It makes unstable params skippable." Senior: gives both changes, the === rule, the version caveat, and the stale-UI migration risk.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Enabling the flag on a legacy app exposed a model with a plain var that used to refresh only because recomposition was never skipped.

questions.promptHtml: Under strong skipping, when does Compose use === and when equals(), and what are the consequences?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: The nuance behind most "why does it still recompose" bugs.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Stable parameters are compared with equals(), unstable with ===. So an unstable UiState rebuilt with identical contents recomposes, because it is a new instance, while a stable data class with equal contents skips. The cost trade-off: === is O(1) but misses equal-but-new objects; equals() catches those but can be O(n) for collections.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Consequences:

  • === for unstable means copying state.copy() into a fresh instance on every emission gives no skip.
  • Annotating to force equals() helps only if instances are recreated AND equals is cheap (flat, small).
  • A @Stable model holding a 5,000-element list compares all 5,000 elements each pass; official docs warn this can be slower than recomposing, especially in lazy layouts and when the model is passed through two levels (compared at each).
  • equals() on a data class is generated; deep nested models compare deeply.

Decision table:

Situation Prefer
Same instance preserved upstream leave unstable, === wins
Small flat model re-created with equal values @Immutable/config -> equals
Large collection re-created fix allocation upstream; benchmark before annotating

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@Immutable                       // OK: flat, cheap equals
data class Avatar(val id: Long, val url: String)

class FeedState(val items: List<Post>)   // leave unstable; keep instance across emissions

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Annotating big collection holders @Immutable.
  • copy()-ing a state class when nothing changed.
  • Ignoring that nested composables repeat the comparison.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do I keep the instance? → distinctUntilChanged, StateFlow equality, cache in ViewModel.
  2. Does StateFlow dedupe by equals? → Yes, it conflates equal values, which helps if equals is meaningful.
  3. Cost of equals for 5k items? → 5,000 element compares per pass per comparing site; show math against recomposition cost with a benchmark.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: lists the two comparisons. Senior: reasons about allocation upstream, repeated comparison across levels, and benchmarks.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An @Immutable annotation on a model with a 2k-item list added measurable scroll cost; removing it and caching the list instance fixed it.

questions.promptHtml: How does strong skipping memoize lambdas, and how does that differ from a normal remember?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Lambdas are the most frequent hidden cause of "child recomposes for no reason".

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: With strong skipping, the compiler wraps every lambda created inside a composable in a remember keyed by its captured values. If the captures are the same, the same lambda instance is reused, so a child receiving it sees an equal param and can skip. Unlike a hand-written remember, unstable captures are compared by === and stable ones by equals(). @DontMemoize opts a lambda out.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Without memoization, { vm.onClick(item.id) } inside a composable allocates a new object each recomposition. Function-typed params are "stable" but two distinct lambda instances are not equals, so the child saw a changed param and recomposed. The docs stress that lambdas were always considered stable; the problem was allocation.

Compiler rewrite (conceptually):

val onClick = remember(item, vm) { { vm.onClick(item.id) } }

Details:

  • Keys are the lambda's captures; captured State objects count by reference, so a lambda reading state.value inside still sees fresh values (it reads at invocation).
  • Captured plain vals that change (new value each recomposition) change the key and produce a new lambda, correctly.
  • Third-party guidance reports some scopes are not auto-memoized (for example lambdas passed to LazyListScope.items {} content, pointerInput blocks, anonymous object members). Treat as "verify with decompiled output/reports" for your version.
  • Lambdas in non-composable scopes you create yourself are not remembered.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@Composable
fun Row(item: Item, vm: ItemViewModel) {
    // memoized on (item, vm) under strong skipping; before it, allocated each time
    Button(onClick = { vm.select(item.id) }) { Text(item.title) }
}

val l = @DontMemoize { doSomething() }   // opt out

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Capturing a value that changes every frame (e.g., a new List or a scroll offset) and expecting the lambda to be reused.
  • Adding manual remember around lambdas on strong skipping (redundant).
  • Assuming a method reference vm::select behaves identically (it also captures vm; verify in reports).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Pre-2.0.20 fix? → Hoist to remember(keys) { ... } or use stable event handlers from the ViewModel.
  2. Why not memoize everything forever? → Memory/slot-table cost and stale captures if the key set is wrong; hence @DontMemoize.
  3. What if the capture is unstable and re-created each pass? → New key by ===, so new lambda, child recomposes.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "Lambdas are remembered now." Senior: describes keys and comparison rules, the "lambdas were always stable, only unmemoized" nuance, and where memoization does not apply.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Teams removed hundreds of remember { { ... } } wrappers after upgrading and saw no regressions, but also found a lambda capturing a freshly built list defeating memoization.

questions.promptHtml: Why are classes from my data or domain module often unstable in the UI module, and what are the fixes?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Real apps are multi-module; this is the standard production stability leak.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The compiler can only infer stability for a class if the module that defines it was compiled with the Compose compiler (it needs the stability metadata) or the class is annotated or configured. A pure Kotlin data module has none, so its classes look unstable in the UI module. Fixes: apply the Compose compiler (runtime dependency only) to that module, list the classes in the stability config, annotate with @Stable/@Immutable, or map to UI models in the UI module.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
The compiler runs per module. For a class from a dependency without metadata, it must assume the worst. Under strong skipping this is no longer fatal: the type is compared by ===. It matters when the data layer re-creates equal small objects constantly.

Options, with trade-offs:

Option Pro Con
Compose compiler plugin on data module automatic inference adds runtime dep to a pure-Kotlin module
Stability config file entries no code change, covers external types (java.time) opt-in contract, easy to over-apply
@Stable/@Immutable explicit needs compose-runtime annotations dependency (or compose-runtime-annotation, verify availability)
UI wrapper/mapper clean layering, can precompute display strings allocation + boilerplate

Check results in classes.txt of the module that defines the class and composables.txt of the consumer.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// UI module: wrap domain model into a flat, cheap-equals UI model
@Immutable
data class OrderUi(val id: Long, val title: String, val priceText: String)

fun Order.toUi() = OrderUi(id, title, formatter.format(price))

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Fixing it by annotating huge domain aggregates.
  • Applying the plugin to the module but forgetting the build cache/reports are per module.
  • Using java.time types in UI state directly.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does the Compose plugin on a Kotlin library module add Compose UI? → No, only the runtime dependency (per docs).
  2. Why map to UI models? → Precompute formatting off the main thread, flat stable models, decouple layers.
  3. What breaks if you configure a mutable type as stable? → Stale UI, since mutations are silent.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "Add @Immutable." Senior: compares four options, notes strong skipping softened the problem, and decides by allocation patterns plus a benchmark.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A feed module's domain models lost skippability when the model module was split out; a mapper to UI models fixed it and also moved date formatting off the main thread.

questions.promptHtml: What is the stability configuration file, how do you set it up, and what are its limits?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Shows you know the escape hatch for classes you do not own.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: It is a plain text file listing fully qualified class names (with * and ** wildcards over whole package segments) that the compiler should treat as stable. Available from Compose Compiler 1.5.5. You pass it via stabilityConfigurationFile in the composeCompiler block, per module or shared from the root. It is an unchecked contract, so only list truly immutable or state-observed types.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
File format (comments with //):

java.time.LocalDateTime
com.example.domain.model.*
com.example.domain.**
kotlinx.collections.immutable.*
com.example.GenericClass<*,_>
  • * matches one package segment level, ** includes subpackages. Partial name patterns like *Model are not supported.
  • Generic type params: * means "stable regardless", _ means "ignore" (per docs example, verify exact semantics).
  • Each module compiles separately, so every module that consumes the types needs the config.
  • Gradle:
composeCompiler {
    stabilityConfigurationFile = rootProject.layout.projectDirectory.file("stability_config.conf")
}

Under strong skipping, a listed type switches from === to equals(); for collection holders this can add O(n) compare cost (see Q049).

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Adding kotlin.collections.* to the file for "free skipping", causing element-wise equals everywhere.
  • Forgetting to commit/share the file so modules diverge.
  • Listing mutable types.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Config vs annotation? → Config for types you cannot edit; annotation for your own.
  2. How verify it worked? → The param flips to stable in composables.txt.
  3. Risk of ** on a data package? → One mutable class in it silently becomes "stable" and stale-UI prone.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "A file where you list stable classes." Senior: wildcard semantics, per-module wiring, equality-cost trade-off, and review ownership of the file.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: One shared config in the root repo plus a CODEOWNERS rule prevented ad-hoc ** entries that had caused a stale-UI bug.

questions.promptHtml: When does kotlinx.collections.immutable actually help Compose performance, and when does it hurt?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests whether you can resist cargo-cult fixes.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: ImmutableList is recognized as stable, so params typed with it use equals(). That helps when you cannot preserve the instance and the list is small. It hurts for large lists: each recomposition pass does an element-by-element equals, possibly at several levels. Under strong skipping, a plain List with a stable instance skips in O(1), so my default is to fix allocation and only use immutable collections when a benchmark says so.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Conversions have costs: toImmutableList() copies unless already immutable; persistentListOf builders use a persistent vector (tries), with log-ish update cost and different memory behavior than ArrayList.

Math: list of 2,000 items, each equals ~50 ns for a flat data class -> ~100 us per compare. Compared at 3 sites per frame while scrolling at 60 fps = 0.3 ms of a 16.7 ms budget (illustrative; measure). A skipped lightweight composable might cost less than that.

Where it genuinely helps: a small list (under ~50) rebuilt on every emission by an upstream you do not control; or pre-2.0.20 builds without strong skipping where it was the only way to be skippable.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@Composable
fun Chips(tags: ImmutableList<String>) {   // small list, equality check cheap
    Row { tags.forEach { Chip(it) } }
}
// ViewModel: keep conversion out of composition
val tags: StateFlow<ImmutableList<String>> = repo.tags.map { it.toImmutableList() }.stateIn(...)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Calling toImmutableList() in the composable body (new instance each recomposition and copy cost).
  • Putting ImmutableList in a data class and passing the class and the list down (double compare).
  • Using it for 10k-row lists.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Is persistentListOf same as ImmutableList? → PersistentList extends ImmutableList with efficient copy-on-write updates.
  2. Domain layer leaking this library? → Convert at the UI-state boundary.
  3. Alternative to the library? → @Immutable class Items(val list: List<X>) wrapper (same equality cost caveat).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "Use ImmutableList for stability." Senior: quantifies equality cost, says where to convert, and prefers instance preservation.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A migration to ImmutableList everywhere raised scroll cost on a 3k-item screen until reverted to cached plain lists.

questions.promptHtml: How do @JvmInline value class parameters interact with stability and skipping?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Edge-case knowledge; checks that you know to verify instead of guess.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A value class is stable when the type it wraps is stable, so value class UserId(val raw: Long) is stable and compared by value. Compose's own Dp, Color and TextUnit are value classes. The traps are boxing when it is used as a generic or nullable type, and the compiler/runtime handling varying by version, so I confirm with the compiler report.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: A value class is erased to its underlying type in signatures where possible; $changed logic compares the underlying primitive, which is cheap and avoids allocation. When boxed (nullable UserId?, generics like List<UserId>, passed as Any), an instance is allocated; equals still works by value. Wrapping an unstable type (value class Names(val l: List<String>)) is unstable. Historical issues existed in older compiler versions around value class parameters and default args (verify against the release notes of your Compose compiler, I did not find a current official statement in the stability docs). Use value classes to make IDs type-safe without cost; they do not make an unstable inner type stable.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@JvmInline value class UserId(val raw: Long)        // stable, cheap
@JvmInline value class Names(val list: List<String>) // unstable: wraps List

@Composable fun Profile(id: UserId) { /* skippable by value */ }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Assuming wrapping fixes instability.
  • Overusing nullable value classes on hot paths (boxing).
  • Adding @Immutable unnecessarily.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How is a Dp param compared? → By its underlying float bits, no allocation.
  2. Does @JvmInline matter on Android? → Required for value classes on the JVM.
  3. How would you confirm behavior on your version? → Read classes.txt/composables.txt for a test composable.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "Value classes are lightweight." Senior: stability follows the wrapped type, notes boxing and version uncertainty, verifies with reports.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Switching Long IDs to value classes gave type safety with no recomposition change, confirmed by identical skip counts.

questions.promptHtml: Is making every composable skippable a good goal? When would you use @NonSkippableComposable or @NonRestartableComposable?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Senior judgment: refusing premature optimization with mechanism.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: No. A skippable composable stores every param in the slot table and compares each on every parent recomposition. If the composable is cheap, rarely recomposes, only calls other skippable composables, or has many params or expensive equals, the check can cost more than just running it. Official docs say so explicitly. I use @NonSkippableComposable for restartable but never-skip, and @NonRestartableComposable for tiny wrappers where a recompose scope adds overhead.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Per-skippable cost: extra slot per param, changed() comparison, group bookkeeping, $changed bits in the signature. Per-restartable cost: a RecomposeScope object and updateScope lambda registered at the end of the function.

Decision guide:

Composable shape Choice
Heavy body, stable-ish params, recomposes often skippable (default)
Thin wrapper that just forwards to a Layout/other composable @NonRestartableComposable
Expensive equals params (big models) @NonSkippableComposable or leave unstable (===)
Rare/one-shot screen root do not bother

Better levers than skipping: defer state reads to layout/draw (lambda modifiers), move heavy work out of composition, reduce what a scope reads.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@NonRestartableComposable
@Composable
fun Spacer16() = Spacer(Modifier.height(16.dp))

@NonSkippableComposable
@Composable
fun BigHeader(model: HugeModel) { /* equals too costly */ }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using these annotations without measurement.
  • Applying @NonRestartableComposable to a function that reads state (it then invalidates its caller scope).
  • Chasing a "100% skippable" metric.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What does non-restartable change about state reads? → Reads invalidate the enclosing restartable parent instead.
  2. Do inline composables get scopes? → No (inline composables like Row are non-restartable).
  3. How do you prove overhead? → Macrobenchmark plus composition tracing comparing the two variants.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "Skip as much as possible." Senior: states the per-param bookkeeping cost, lists cases to avoid it, and prioritizes read deferral.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A "make everything skippable" initiative added @Immutable broadly and regressed a list screen's scroll p95; the team reverted the heavy-model cases.

questions.promptHtml: What changed for stability and skipping across Compose compiler versions and with the Kotlin 2.0 compiler plugin?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Version awareness; seniors maintain upgrade paths.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The Compose compiler moved into the Kotlin repo with Kotlin 2.0, shipping as a Kotlin compiler plugin with a Gradle plugin (org.jetbrains.kotlin.plugin.compose), so its version equals the Kotlin version and you no longer pin a separate kotlinCompilerExtensionVersion. Strong skipping was opt-in before and became default in Kotlin 2.0.20. The stability config file arrived in compiler 1.5.5. Always confirm per release notes.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Timeline as I can support it (verify exact numbers against release notes before quoting):

  • Compose Compiler 1.5.4/1.5.x: strong skipping experimental flag (sources differ on the exact patch).
  • 1.5.5: stability configuration file (official docs).
  • Kotlin 2.0.0: compiler plugin in Kotlin repo, new K2 frontend; strong skipping still opt-in.
  • Kotlin 2.0.20: strong skipping on by default (official docs).
  • Reports/metrics are configured via the composeCompiler { } extension (reportsDestination, metricsDestination). Practical effects of upgrading: skippable counts jump; code relying on recomposition side effects or silent mutation breaks; remembered-lambda boilerplate becomes redundant; stability inference may differ subtly between compiler versions, so diff reports across the upgrade.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// build.gradle.kts (module)
plugins {
    alias(libs.plugins.kotlin.android)
    alias(libs.plugins.kotlin.compose)   // org.jetbrains.kotlin.plugin.compose, version = Kotlin version
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Mixing an old composeOptions { kotlinCompilerExtensionVersion } with the new plugin.
  • Not diffing reports before and after an upgrade.
  • Quoting a version from a blog as fact.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you disable strong skipping on 2.0.20+? → Via the plugin's feature flags (verify the exact DSL for your plugin version).
  2. Why does Kotlin and Compose version coupling matter? → One matching toolchain; no compatibility table.
  3. Upgrade strategy? → Branch, report diff, macrobenchmark before/after, staged rollout.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "Upgrade Kotlin and Compose." Senior: knows the timeline, marks uncertainty, and has a measurable upgrade checklist.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A Kotlin upgrade silently turned strong skipping on and exposed a stale-UI bug in a @Stable-annotated class with a plain var.

questions.promptHtml: Mechanically, how does a skippable composable decide to skip? What does the compiler generate?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Staff-level internals: connecting stability to generated code.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The compiler adds a $changed int parameter carrying 3 bits per param (uncertain, same, different, static). At function entry, a generated check compares each param against what is stored in the slot table using Composer.changed(...) (or skips the check if the caller already proved it static/same). If all are unchanged and the function is skippable, it calls skipToGroupEnd() instead of running the body. Stability decides which comparison the check performs.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Sketch of generated code:

fun Child(a: Int, b: Foo, $composer, $changed) {
  $composer.startRestartGroup(KEY)
  dirty = $changed
  if ($changed & 0b0110 == 0) dirty |= if ($composer.changed(a)) 0b0010 else 0b0100
  ... same for b (stable: equals; unstable under strong skipping: ===)
  if (dirty & 0b011011 != 0b010010 || !$composer.skipping) {
      body...
  } else {
      $composer.skipToGroupEnd()
  }
  $composer.endRestartGroup()?.updateScope { c, _ -> Child(a, b, c, $changed or 1) }
}
  • Callers pass "static" info for literals and constants, letting the callee skip the comparison entirely.
  • endRestartGroup returns the scope used to re-invoke on invalidation (restartability).
  • The skip decision is positional: stored param values live in the slot table at that call site.
  • Function body also not run if the invalidated scope is a child only; parent skipping prevents the entire subtree re-execution.

sections.label: Code
sections.html: Read decompiled output via Kotlin bytecode viewer, or reports; do not hand-write this.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Thinking skipping is a runtime heuristic. It is generated code.
  • Forgetting default params add $default mask logic.
  • Believing $changed is exposed API (it is internal; do not rely on it).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What does the static bit save? → The compare for literals/constants.
  2. Why does parameter count matter? → More compares, bits (31/3 ~10 params per $changed int, a second int is added beyond that; approximate, verify).
  3. How does strong skipping alter this? → Unstable params use === instead of "always changed" marks.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "Compose compares params." Senior: describes $changed bit-packing, slot-table storage, skipToGroupEnd, and static propagation.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Understanding this explained why a composable with 14 params was slow to skip, motivating a grouped params class.

questions.promptHtml: A composable is marked skippable and its params are unchanged, yet it still recomposes. How can that be?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Separates the two invalidation channels: parent-driven (params) and state-read-driven.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Skipping only applies when the parent recomposes and calls the child. A composable also recomposes when a State it read in its own scope changes, and that bypasses the param check. Other causes: a CompositionLocal it reads changed, params did change (new instance of an unstable value, new lambda capture), or the "skippable" function is invoked from a non-skippable caller.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Two invalidation paths:

Path A (parent):  parent scope invalidated -> re-calls child -> param check -> skip or run
Path B (own read): child read State.value -> that State written -> child scope invalidated directly -> runs, no param check
Path C: CompositionLocal.current read -> provider value changed -> readers invalidated

So Layout Inspector "recomposed" counts can be legitimate. Debug order: (1) does the child read state itself? (2) did a param change by ===/equals? (3) is a local read? (4) did a key change or the node move (new identity => recreated, not recomposed)?

Using lambda-deferred reads (Modifier.offset { }, graphicsLayer { }) moves path B out of composition into layout/draw.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@Composable
fun Child(label: String, scroll: State<Int>) {
    // reads scroll in composition: recomposes on every change regardless of label being same
    Text("$label ${scroll.value}")
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Assuming parameter equality implies no recomposition.
  • Passing State<T> where a lambda () -> T would defer reads.
  • Not noticing a local read.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How find the read? → Layout Inspector recomposition highlighting plus reading the code for .value/by delegates; composition tracing.
  2. Does the parent also recompose? → Compare counts: parent unchanged but child incrementing means path B.
  3. Does derivedStateOf help? → Only reduces invalidations when output changes less often than input.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "Params must have changed." Senior: three invalidation channels and a debugging order.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A badge composable recomposed every frame because it read a scroll State directly; passing a lambda moved the read to the layout phase.

questions.promptHtml: On a codebase still on Compose compiler 1.5.x without strong skipping, how do lambdas cause missed skips, and how do you fix them?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Many large apps are stuck on older toolchains; seniors must handle both worlds.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Lambdas are stable, but a lambda that captures an unstable value (or a non-stable var/ViewModel reference) is re-allocated each recomposition, so the child sees a new instance and recomposes. Fixes: capture only stable values, hoist the lambda into remember(keys), use a method reference on a stable receiver, or pass IDs with a single stable callback (Id) -> Unit. Enabling strong skipping is the real fix.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Old compiler memoized a lambda only if all captures were stable. Unstable captures (a List, an unannotated class, a ViewModel) meant a new instance every pass.

Patterns:

// Bad: captures `vm` (unstable) and `item`; new lambda each recomposition
ItemRow(item, onClick = { vm.onClick(item.id) })

// Good: one stable callback, item passed as data
@Composable fun List(items: List<Item>, onClick: (Long) -> Unit) {
    LazyColumn { items(items, key = { it.id }) { ItemRow(it, onClick) } }
}

Hoisting onClick as a single stable function type avoids per-item lambdas. Also remember(vm) { { id: Long -> vm.onClick(id) } }. A ViewModel exposing val onClick: (Long) -> Unit stable property also works.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• remember without keys that actually capture changing values (stale callback).
  • Capturing State.value in a lambda created in composition (reads late, which is usually fine, but capturing the snapshot value freezes it).
  • Believing method references are always memoized.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Is remember { {..} } safe with a changing capture? → Only with keys or rememberUpdatedState (stale otherwise).
  2. Why do ViewModel captures hurt? → ViewModel is unstable, so the lambda was not memoized.
  3. What replaces this after the upgrade? → Delete boilerplate; compiler remembers by captures.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "Wrap in remember." Senior: explains allocation vs stability, stale-capture risk, and the single-callback pattern.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A 50-row list recomposed all rows on any state change because each row got a fresh lambda capturing the ViewModel.

questions.contextHtml:
Strong skipping is on (Kotlin 2.0.21). A product list screen: 300 items, 90 DAU-thousand users. Layout Inspector shows every ProductRow recomposing about 40 times per second while a countdown timer in the header ticks every 100 ms. The QA device mix is mostly mid-tier phones, scroll p95 frame time 24 ms. Code:

@Composable
fun ProductScreen(vm: ProductVm) {
    val products by vm.products.collectAsStateWithLifecycle()
    val remaining by vm.countdown.collectAsStateWithLifecycle()
    Column {
        Header(remaining)
        ProductList(products.filter { it.inStock })
    }
}

ProductList(items: List<Product>) is restartable skippable in the report with unstable items.
questions.promptHtml: Why do rows recompose with a 100 ms timer, and how do you fix it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "The list is unstable, use ImmutableList." That ignores strong skipping and the real allocation in the call.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which Kotlin version (is strong skipping on)? Does Product have a cheap equals? Is the timer state read in the same scope as the list? How many items are in view?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Hoist the filter out with remember so the timer no longer triggers new list allocation.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) products.filter {} allocates a new list on each ProductScreen recomposition (timer read here recomposes the whole scope) so === fails; (b) rows read the timer; (c) unkeyed items; (d) red herring: Product instability.
  4. How I'd verify: Layout Inspector counts: header and ProductList both ticking; Compose report shows skippable; add a log of items.hashCode() identity.
  5. Root cause: remaining is read in ProductScreen's scope, so every tick recomposes it, re-running filter and creating a new List instance; unstable param compared by === fails; list recomposes.
  6. Fix: Short-term: val visible = remember(products) { products.filter { it.inStock } }. Long-term: push inStock filtering into the ViewModel, expose one StateFlow<List<Product>>, and read remaining only inside Header via a lambda () -> Int or a separate composable collecting it.
  7. Prevention: Review rule "no collection transforms in composition"; Layout Inspector check on timer/animation screens; report diff in CI.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not wrap in ImmutableList (adds copy and O(n) equals each tick, 300 items * 10 ticks/s) and not annotate Product.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if the list is 5,000 items? → Same fix; additionally paginate and key by id so scrolling stays bounded.
  • What if strong skipping were off? → The unstable param would make ProductList non-skippable even with remember; enable it or wrap list.
  • What if remaining must stay in the screen scope? → Pass { remaining } lambda to Header so only it reads.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A launch-day countdown banner made the whole catalog recompose ten times a second; moving one .value read into the banner dropped CPU use by a third.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames List stability, proposes ImmutableList.
  • Hire: spots the new list instance per tick and hoists with remember.
  • Strong hire: also isolates the timer read scope, quantifies the cost, and rejects annotation fixes.

questions.contextHtml:
A settings screen shows a user's notification toggles. After merging a refactor, the switches no longer visually update when tapped, though the backend value changes (confirmed in logs). Crash-free is 99.9%; only this screen is affected. The model:

@Stable
class NotificationPrefs(
    var email: Boolean,
    var push: Boolean,
)

@Composable
fun PrefsCard(prefs: NotificationPrefs, onToggle: () -> Unit) {
    Switch(checked = prefs.push, onCheckedChange = { prefs.push = it; onToggle() })
}

It worked before the Kotlin 1.9 to 2.0.21 upgrade.
questions.promptHtml: Explain why it broke and fix it.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Compose is buggy after the upgrade, downgrade." Misses that the contract was always violated.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Did the upgrade change strong skipping? Is prefs the same instance each time? Is there any other state read?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Make the toggle use state, or copy into a new immutable object on change.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) @Stable lie: plain var mutated with no notification; (b) parent not recomposing since params look the same; (c) lambda memoization stale; (d) red herring: backend sync.
  4. How I'd verify: Layout Inspector: toggle tapped, PrefsCard count unchanged; report shows skippable; reproduce with a unit-level composition test.
  5. Root cause: @Stable promises change notification; the plain var mutates silently. With the old toolchain something else (non-memoized lambda, unstable paths) caused incidental recomposition; strong skipping now skips because the same instance is passed and annotated equals/identity is unchanged.
  6. Fix: Use var push by mutableStateOf(...) inside the class, or immutable data class with copy held in MutableStateFlow. Remove the annotation if it was only added for silence.
  7. Prevention: Lint/review rule for @Stable classes: every public var must be state-backed; test that toggles update; run report diffs on upgrades.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not @DontMemoize or @NonSkippableComposable hacks: they hide the contract bug.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why did it work before? → Old compiler recomposed more often (non-memoized lambdas), masking the lie.
  • Can I keep the mutable class? → Yes, with state-backed properties.
  • Could @Immutable help? → It would be a worse lie.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A toolchain upgrade made a long-hidden @Stable violation visible as frozen toggles; the team added a custom lint check for state-backed vars.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames the upgrade.
  • Hire: identifies the violated contract and fixes with state.
  • Strong hire: explains why masking happened before and adds prevention.

questions.contextHtml: A news app (4.2M MAU, mid-tier Android devices at 50% of traffic) shipped a Kotlin 2.0.21 upgrade. Frame metrics from field data (JankStats) show jank rate for the home feed rising from 6% to 14% and p95 frame time from 19 ms to 31 ms on devices with 3 GB RAM. Crash/ANR rates unchanged. The feed uses LazyColumn with 400 ArticleUi items; the team had added @Immutable to FeedState (holding List<ArticleUi>) in a prior sprint plus kotlin.collections.* in stability_config.conf "for strong skipping".
questions.promptHtml: Diagnose and fix without reverting the upgrade.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add more annotations or Baseline Profiles" without evidence.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What exactly changed with the release (toolchain, config, content)? Does regression correlate with feed length? Is it only scroll or also first display? Are item models re-created on each emission?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Ship a config revert via remote flag if available; otherwise hotfix removing the collection wildcard and the @Immutable on FeedState.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) element-wise equals on 400-item lists at several levels, now forced by config; (b) new instance churn from mapping in ViewModel; (c) strong skipping revealing new recompositions; (d) red herring: R8 changes.
  4. How I'd verify: Macrobenchmark FrameTimingMetric before/after config; composition trace sections show equals time in changed(); report diff shows unstable to stable for List params.
  5. Root cause: Config and annotation made lists "stable" so Compose runs equals across 400 ArticleUi objects each recomposition pass and again in nested composables, adding CPU on slow devices.
  6. Fix: Remove kotlin.collections.* and @Immutable on holders; rely on === and keep the list instance cached in the ViewModel with distinctUntilChanged; annotate only flat ArticleUi if equals is cheap.
  7. Prevention: Macrobenchmark gate on feed scroll; CODEOWNERS on stability config; report diffs.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not disable strong skipping globally; it fixed other screens.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Ten times the items? → Cost scales linearly; paging is mandatory.
  • Why mid-tier only? → CPU-bound compares; fast devices hide it.
  • What if elements are re-created per emission? → Fix upstream mapping; if impossible, benchmark equals vs recompose per item.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A well-intentioned "make lists stable" change moved cost from rendering into equality checks; the data showed it only on low-RAM devices.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: random fixes.
  • Hire: ties regression to forced equals, reverts config.
  • Strong hire: validates with benchmark, plans gating, and explains device-class skew.

questions.contextHtml: Your org has a :core:model module (pure Kotlin, 180 data classes, used by backend sync, Room, and UI), a :feature:* UI layer in Compose with ~35 screens, and Kotlin 2.0.21. The report for feature modules shows 60% of composables with unstable model params. Strong skipping is on. Feature teams propose three options: A) enable the Compose compiler plugin on :core:model; B) add com.example.core.model.** to the stability config; C) introduce UI models per screen. A manager wants a decision by next sprint.
questions.promptHtml: Which do you choose and why?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Picks B because it is a one-line change, with no analysis of mutability.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Are the models immutable (val, no mutable collections)? How often does the data layer re-create equal instances? Which screens are hot? Are there Room entities in there?
  2. Immediate mitigation: None needed under strong skipping; no incident. First measure, not change.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) most screens do not need change since === works; (b) a few hot lists suffer from instance churn; (c) models contain vars or mutable lists making ** dangerous; (d) red herring: raw unstable counts.
  4. How I'd verify: Layout Inspector counts on top 5 screens; macrobenchmark; classes report from :core:model to see why each class is unstable.
  5. Root cause: Missing Compose metadata in the model module, so inference gives up.
  6. Fix: Decision: C for the hot screens (flat UI models with preformatted strings, cheap equals), A only if :core:model is already immutable and the team accepts the runtime dependency; avoid B's ** because one mutable class becomes silently stale-prone.
  7. Prevention: Immutability convention for models, review of config, report diff in CI.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not annotate everything; not wrap collections in immutable types before benchmarks.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Mapper allocation cost? → One per emission, off the main thread; negligible vs recompose savings.
  • What if models have vars? → Do not use A or B; fix the models first.
  • Kotlin Multiplatform shared module? → Plugin on a KMP module is possible but adds a Compose runtime dependency across targets; prefer UI mappers.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: Per-screen UI models also deleted a dozen "format in composable" bugs, which was a bigger win than skipping.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: picks option by effort.
  • Hire: compares options by mutability and churn.
  • Strong hire: measures first, ties choice to benchmarks, and sets conventions.

questions.contextHtml: A chat screen renders LazyColumn of MessageUi(id, text, sender, reactions: List<Reaction>). Today channels have about 200 messages; a new "large community" product will push 5,000 to 20,000 messages in memory, with new messages arriving at 5/s. Strong skipping is on. Current p95 frame time is 12 ms on a Pixel 6 class device and 22 ms on a 3 GB device. Someone proposes @Immutable on MessageUi and ImmutableList<MessageUi> everywhere "to be safe at scale".
questions.promptHtml: How do you make this scale, and do you accept the proposal?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Accepts, since immutable is "obviously faster".

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the whole list held in memory? Does each arrival rebuild the list? Is the list wrapped by a model passed to many composables? What is the distribution of visible items?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Cap in-memory window and page; none of this needs stability changes.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) per-arrival list rebuild causes new instance, but only visible items compose in lazy lists, so cost is equals/diff, not item count; (b) ImmutableList equals compares 20k elements on every pass; (c) reactions list inside each item is unstable; (d) red herring: item count in composition.
  4. How I'd verify: Macrobenchmark with synthetic 20k list at 5 msgs/s; composition trace; Layout Inspector counts on visible rows.
  5. Root cause (of the risk): Equality across 20k elements is O(n) per compare and per level (5 msgs/s * several compare sites); lazy layout only composes visible items, but a stable-annotated list holder would still run equals on all.
  6. Fix: Windowed paging (Paging 3 or custom), key = { it.id }, contentType, append-only updates keeping prior item instances (structural sharing: only the new message is a new object), flat MessageUi with cheap equals annotated if the data layer re-creates it; reactions as a single summary string/count to avoid nested lists.
  7. Prevention: Scale benchmark in CI at 20k; budget test on the low-end device.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not annotate the list holder or use ImmutableList for the 20k list.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if each arrival copies the list? → ArrayList copy of 20k refs is cheap (about tens of microseconds); equality is the expensive part, so === mode with new instance recomposes the parent only, not each item.
  • Why still recompose rows? → Rows skip by their own params (same item instances).
  • How handle edits in the middle? → Replace only that element; others keep identity.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: Structural sharing of message objects reduced recomposition on arrival to exactly one row, regardless of channel size.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: accepts blanket immutability.
  • Hire: identifies O(n) equality risk and uses keys/paging.
  • Strong hire: relies on identity preservation and benchmarks at target scale.

questions.contextHtml: A 6M-DAU app is on Kotlin 1.9.24 with Compose Compiler 1.5.14 and 25 modules. Leadership wants strong skipping to cut jank. There is a weekly release train with 5% staged rollout, a Macrobenchmark suite on two devices, and a known 3% crash-free regression budget threshold of 0.1%. The code base contains a handful of @Stable classes of unknown correctness and many remember { { } } lambdas.
questions.promptHtml: How do you roll it out safely?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Flip enableStrongSkippingMode = true globally and ship."

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Can I enable per module? Is there UI test coverage on the key flows? Are the flags available in my compiler version (the DSL differs)? Which modules own the hot screens?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Not applicable; plan staged change with a rollback (revert commit, since it is compile-time not runtime).
  3. Hypotheses, ranked (what could go wrong): (a) stale UI from state-unsafe models (@Stable lies, plain vars) once skipping occurs; (b) behavior relying on lambdas re-allocating; (c) CPU overhead of more comparisons in huge param lists; (d) red herring: APK size (docs: roughly +4 kB in a sample app).
  4. How I'd verify: Report diff per module; Macrobenchmark before/after; UI tests on state-driven screens; internal dogfood build.
  5. Root cause (of risk): Skipping now happens where it previously could not.
  6. Fix/plan: Enable module by module starting with leaf feature modules (composeCompiler { enableStrongSkippingMode = true } in Kotlin <2.0.20; after Kotlin 2.0.20 it is default, so the upgrade itself is the change); audit @Stable classes first; keep remember lambdas until stable; ship in a regular 5% train; watch JankStats and crash rates for a week.
  7. Prevention: Lint for @Stable class var; benchmark gate.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not combine with a Kotlin upgrade and a design change in the same release (cannot attribute regressions).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Rollback story? → Compile-time, so rollback means a new release or hotfix; hence staged rollout and dogfood.
  • A module crashes in release only? → Check R8/obfuscation of remember keys is unrelated; bisect modules with the flag.
  • Can I disable for one function? → @NonSkippableComposable.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: An audit of @Stable types before enabling caught three silent-mutation classes that would have shipped as stale-UI bugs.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: flips it globally.
  • Hire: audits annotated classes and stages by module.
  • Strong hire: separates changes, defines metrics and rollback.

questions.contextHtml: Post-incident: after a release, an e-commerce cart screen's p95 frame time went from 14 ms to 28 ms, and "Add to cart" taps felt delayed by about 200 ms on 30% of devices (2022-era mid-tier). Timeline: a refactor replaced onAddToCart: (Long) -> Unit with per-row lambdas { vm.add(item, selectedVariant, promo) }, where promo is a PromoInfo produced by a function called in composition (vm.currentPromo(), new object each call). Rollback fixed it within hours. Strong skipping is on. The team asks for a blameless review.
questions.promptHtml: What was the mechanism, and what are the corrective actions?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Lambdas are bad; avoid lambdas."

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What does currentPromo() return and how often is it called? How many rows are visible? Was this caught by any benchmark?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Done: rollback. Interim: keep one callback with an ID.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) lambda key includes a new PromoInfo instance each pass so memoization misses; (b) every row's lambda changes so every row recomposes; (c) heavy logic in currentPromo(); (d) red herring: Add-to-cart network call.
  4. How I'd verify: Layout Inspector: all rows incrementing at every parent recomposition; trace section durations; report shows lambda captures.
  5. Root cause: Memoization keys by captures with === for unstable ones; a freshly allocated capture is never === to the previous one, so lambdas never reused; children received "new" params and recomposed, 20 visible rows * heavy bodies.
  6. Fix: Capture IDs and read promo inside the click path: onAdd(item.id) with val promo by vm.promo.collectAsStateWithLifecycle() read once; or remember(promoId) stable capture.
  7. Prevention: Review rule: never capture values produced by calls in composition; benchmark on cart screen; add Compose trace markers; runbook for rollback.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not @DontMemoize, which would worsen allocation; not blame the author.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why only 30% of devices? → CPU-bound; recomposition cost scales with slow cores.
  • Could a lint catch it? → A custom detector for calls like vm.xxx() in composables passed into lambdas (partial).
  • Would stable PromoInfo fix it? → Equal values but new instance would pass if equals is used (annotated), still better to avoid creation.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: The cart regression showed that the "per-item lambda" pattern is safe only when captures are identity-stable.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: vague "lambdas allocate".
  • Hire: explains captures-by-identity and fixes by ID callback.
  • Strong hire: includes blameless corrective actions and detection gaps.

questions.contextHtml: A new engineering director sets an OKR: "100% of composables skippable, enforced by a CI check on compiler reports." The app has 1,800 composables; today 71% are skippable (strong skipping on). To hit the metric, one team proposes adding @Immutable to every model, and ImmutableList everywhere. Another notes that recomposition counts on the heaviest screens are already low.
questions.promptHtml: How do you respond to the OKR?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Executes the OKR literally.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What outcome is the OKR meant to serve (jank, CPU, battery)? What is the current jank rate and which screens drive it? Why are 29% non-skippable (non-restartable? inline? intentionally)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Propose to replace the metric with an outcome metric before work begins.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) most non-skippable ones are inline/non-restartable and irrelevant; (b) annotation blast would add equals overhead; (c) a few hot screens have real issues; (d) red herring: skippable percentage correlates with user experience.
  4. How I'd verify: Break down the 29% from CSV by cause; Macrobenchmark and JankStats per screen; trace the top screens.
  5. Root cause: The proxy metric is not the goal; docs state skipping has its own cost and not every composable should be skippable.
  6. Fix: Propose targets: p95 frame time and jank rate per top-10 screens; a "no regression" report diff check instead of 100%; fix hot screens with read deferral, instance preservation, keys.
  7. Prevention: Macrobenchmark in CI; dashboard from JankStats field data; short stability guidelines.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not blanket annotations; not forcing @NonRestartableComposable to game the metric.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Director insists? → Offer a scoped metric: skippable for list-item composables on the top screens.
  • Who owns exceptions? → A documented allowlist with justification.
  • Gaming risk? → Annotations make metric green and perf worse; Goodhart.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: Switching an OKR from "percent skippable" to "feed p95 frame time" redirected effort to a single unkeyed list that gave a 30% win.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: complies.
  • Hire: challenges the metric with doc-backed cost.
  • Strong hire: proposes outcome metrics and an exception process.

questions.contextHtml: A teammate's PR adds @Immutable to 14 classes with the description "fixes recomposition". The classes include a UserProfile (flat, 6 fields), a SearchResults(val items: List<Result>, val query: String), a FormState(var name: String, var errors: MutableList<String>), and an OrderUi containing a LocalDate. There is no benchmark or report in the PR. You are the reviewer with 20 minutes.
questions.promptHtml: What do you say in review, class by class?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Approve because "immutable is good".

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is strong skipping on? Which screens regressed, and what evidence shows recomposition cost? Where do these classes live (Compose-compiled module)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Block merge until there is a report or trace showing the problem.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: per class: (a) UserProfile probably already inferred stable if module compiled with plugin: annotation is noise; (b) SearchResults annotation forces element-wise equals; (c) FormState violates the contract (mutable vars, MutableList): a bug; (d) OrderUi with LocalDate needs config or a string field.
  4. How I'd verify: Run compiler report before/after; check classes.txt; Layout Inspector counts.
  5. Root cause: Annotation used as a switch instead of a contract.
  6. Fix: Remove annotations from inferred-stable and collection-holding classes; rewrite FormState as immutable plus copy, or state-backed; replace LocalDate with display text or add to config if appropriate.
  7. Prevention: PR template requiring report diff; a lint rule banning @Immutable on classes with var or mutable collections.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not approve and plan to measure later; not rewrite the PR for them without discussing.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• They show a benchmark win on one class? → Accept that one with the numbers noted in the PR.
  • What if UserProfile is in a non-Compose module? → Annotation or config is justified only if instances are recreated frequently.
  • @Stable instead of @Immutable for FormState? → Only with state-backed fields.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A single @Immutable on a class with a mutable list produced a stale search result list that took a day to find.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: approves.
  • Hire: flags FormState contract violation and asks for evidence.
  • Strong hire: goes class by class with report-based justification and prevention.

questions.contextHtml:
On a profile screen, StatsCard is restartable skippable in the report, all params stable, yet Layout Inspector shows it recomposing about 60 times per second when the user scrolls the parent Column(Modifier.verticalScroll(state)). Frame time at p95 is 19 ms on a 60 Hz device. Code:

@Composable
fun Profile(state: ScrollState, stats: Stats) {
    Column(Modifier.verticalScroll(state)) {
        StatsCard(stats, scrollOffset = state.value)
        Details(stats)
    }
}

Details shows 0 recompositions.
questions.promptHtml: Why is a skippable composable recomposing, and how do you fix it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Make Stats immutable." The report already says stable.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What does scrollOffset drive visually (parallax)? Is state.value read in composition? Is StatsCard the only consumer?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Remove or throttle the offset-driven effect.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) param scrollOffset: Int really changes every frame; skipping correctly not possible; (b) Profile itself recomposes per frame (reads state.value in its scope); (c) Stats unstable; (d) red herring: Column.
  4. How I'd verify: Counts: Profile and StatsCard increment together, Details skipped (its params unchanged), confirming path A with a changing param.
  5. Root cause: Reading state.value in the Profile scope makes that scope invalidate on each scroll tick; scrollOffset differs each time so StatsCard's param check correctly fails. Skippable does not mean skipped.
  6. Fix: Defer the read: pass scrollOffset = { state.value } and use it in Modifier.graphicsLayer { translationY = ... } or offset { } inside StatsCard, so only layout/draw phases rerun.
  7. Prevention: Review rule: animated/scroll values passed as lambdas; Layout Inspector check on scroll screens.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not derivedStateOf (the value truly changes every frame); not memo hacks.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• When is derivedStateOf right? → When you need a coarse output like offset > 0.
  • Would strong skipping change anything? → No; the param changed.
  • What if StatsCard needs the value for text? → Then composition work is needed; throttle updates to coarse steps.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: Moving a parallax read into graphicsLayer {} cut per-frame composition entirely, leaving only draw work.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: pursues stability annotations.
  • Hire: identifies changing param and read scope.
  • Strong hire: defers read via lambda to later phase and cites phases.

questions.contextHtml:
After enabling strong skipping, a checkout screen shows a stale "Total" after the user changes quantity, but only on the second change. Crash-free unchanged; support tickets up 8x in a day; reproducible in about 1 in 3 attempts. The code:

class Cart(val lines: MutableList<Line>)         // not annotated, unstable

@Composable
fun CartScreen(cart: Cart, onQty: (Int, Int) -> Unit) {
    Column {
        cart.lines.forEachIndexed { i, l -> LineRow(l, onQty = { q -> onQty(i, q) }) }
        Total(cart)                               // Total(cart: Cart)
    }
}
// ViewModel: fun onQty(i: Int, q: Int) { cart.lines[i] = cart.lines[i].copy(qty = q); _cart.value = cart }

_cart is a MutableStateFlow<Cart>.
questions.promptHtml: Why is Total stale, and what do you do now and later?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "A Compose bug with strong skipping; turn it off."

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the same Cart instance emitted? Do other fields recompose? Does it reproduce with strong skipping off?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Hotfix: emit a new Cart with a copied list on every change.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) StateFlow sees _cart.value = cart as the same instance (equals true) so no emission; (b) even if emitted, Total(cart) skips since === is the same instance; (c) lambda memoization stale; (d) red herring: threading.
  4. How I'd verify: Log System.identityHashCode(cart); observe no emission; unit test collecting the flow; toggle strong skipping to see old behavior mask the bug.
  5. Root cause: Mutating a shared mutable object and re-publishing the same reference. StateFlow conflates equal values and Compose compares unstable by ===, so nothing signals change. It "worked" before because non-skippable composables always re-ran.
  6. Fix: Immutable Cart(val lines: List<Line>); reducer creates cart.copy(lines = lines.toMutableList().also { it[i] = ... }); emit a new instance each change. Long-term: mutations only in the state holder, single source of truth.
  7. Prevention: Test: change quantity twice and assert total; ban mutable collections in UI state via lint/review; pre-enable audit.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not disable strong skipping; not add @Stable to patch it; not force recomposition with a counter hack.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Could mutableStateListOf work? → Yes, if state-backed and read in composition (see snapshot state chunk).
  • Why second change only? → First change may coincide with another emission that created a new instance.
  • Does StateFlow need equals? → Yes, it dedupes by equals; a data class compare would treat same instance as equal.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: The incident was a latent UI-state mutation bug unmasked by a legitimate compiler optimization; the fix was architectural, not a flag.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: disables strong skipping.
  • Hire: identifies same-instance mutation and fixes with copy.
  • Strong hire: explains StateFlow conflation plus === skip and adds prevention.
